n1: In chat, the agent decides what happens next, every turn. That's wrong for work you want done the same way every time. A workflow hands the control flow to a file instead: what runs, in what order, and when. The agent still works inside it, on a leash the file declares.
n2: Keelson ships starter workflows. The smoke test runs one of every kind of node.
n3: Nine nodes, all green, in a few seconds. Several started at once.
n4: Those nodes come in three families. Agent nodes run model turns: a prompt, a named command, a loop. Deterministic nodes, bash and scripts, run code with no model at all. Control nodes pause for a human, or end a branch on purpose. The mix sets how much is judgment, and how much is fact.
n5: The browser runs the same workflow, and shows the executor at work.
n6: Every node whose dependencies are met starts right away, and the rest start the moment theirs settle.
n7: And both runs are still here: the one from the terminal, and this one.
n8: Because a run is a record. Keelson stores a row for the run and one per node: its output, its timing, the model it really ran on, and a hash of the exact definition. A failed run resumes from the first unfinished node, without redoing finished work.
n9: The file decides. The run remembers.
n10: Keelson. Lay the keel, raise the ribs.
